paragraphs.text: When a supermarket opens on the edge of a town, the small shops in the centre often close within a few years. Many people see this as the natural result of competition, and they are partly right: supermarkets are usually cheaper and more convenient.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: But I believe the loss is greater than the price of a loaf of bread. A street of independent shops keeps people walking in the town centre, and those people also visit cafés, libraries and banks. When the shops go, the whole centre begins to empty.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Local councils have tried to help by lowering business rates for small shops. This is welcome, although in my experience the effect has been modest, because rent rather than tax is usually the heaviest cost.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Shoppers, too, have a part to play. Nobody should feel guilty for buying cheaper goods, but choosing a local shop for a few items each week costs little and matters more than most people realise.
paragraphs.label: D

items.prompt: The writer accepts that supermarkets are often cheaper than small shops.
The writer thinks the closure of small shops affects only their owners.
The writer believes lower business rates have solved the problems of small shops.
The writer thinks councils should limit the rents that landlords charge.
The writer suggests that regularly buying a few items in local shops is worthwhile.
